item.title: From Delhi to Makkah: Bangladesh’s calculated political gamble?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The uncertainty surrounding Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to India and Dhaka’s growing interest in the Makkah Defense Pact are being viewed as possible signs of a shift in Bangladesh’s foreign-policy calculations. But for Tarique Rahman, this is unlikely to be a sudden or whimsical decision. Politically, it appears to be a carefully calculated move.
The proposed India visit has yet to take place, despite an invitation from New Delhi and discussions over possible dates. But the timing has become complicated.
The uncertainty reflects how difficult India-Bangladesh relations have become since Sheikh Hasina was ousted in August 2024 and fled to India.
Her continued stay in India has become one of the biggest contentious issues between the two neighbours. Bangladesh has repeatedly sought her extradition after a tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia in November 2025 over her role in the deadly crackdown on the 2024 student-led uprising. Hasina has rejected the proceedings as politically motivated.
Against this backdrop, anti-India sentiment grew in Bangladesh after the fall of the Awami League government. “Delhi or Dhaka? Dhaka, Dhaka” became a popular political slogan, reflecting a growing perception among sections of the public that Bangladesh should reduce its dependence on India.
But the BNP government cannot simply turn away from New Delhi.
India is Bangladesh’s most important geographical neighbour, sharing a more than 4,000-kilometre border and deep economic, security, and cultural ties. Whatever political differences exist between the two governments, geography makes a working relationship unavoidable.
That makes Rahman’s decision over an India visit particularly sensitive.
On August 5, Hasina, speaking from India in her first media interaction since her ouster, said she intended to return to Bangladesh in December. She said she was prepared to face detention or even death.
Among the questions from journalists was whether she would visit the shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi before returning to Bangladesh. Hasina responded positively.
Visiting religious shrines, particularly Islamic shrines, is not new for Bangladeshi politicians. Before national election campaigns, leaders from major political parties often visit shrines, both as a cultural tradition and as a way of connecting with voters.
Around 90% of Bangladesh’s population is Muslim, and political parties have long sought to tap into religious sentiment when building support for major political moves.
Meanwhile, Hasina’s remarks triggered a sharp reaction from Dhaka, which criticized India for allowing her to address the media from its territory.
For Rahman, visiting India while Hasina remains there therefore carries an obvious political risk.
His government emerged from the political forces that opposed Hasina and her Awami League. A visit to New Delhi at this moment could raise questions among those forces about whether Dhaka was making concessions over Hasina or seeking a political accommodation with India.
It could create mistrust, or even divisions, among the pro-July forces.
Rahman therefore appears to have little political incentive to take that risk at this stage. Instead, he appears intent on keeping the pro-July forces together, despite their differences, as they seek to politically counter the Awami League in the coming days, much as they did in 2024.
And then came another event.
Saudi Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman invited Rahman to visit Saudi Arabia. Saudi Ambassador Abdullah Zafer H bin Abiyah delivered the invitation on August 17.
The invitation came at a time when Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan had signed the much-discussed Makkah Joint Defense Agreement.
Signed in Makkah on August 7, the agreement states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all three, making it similar in principle to NATO’s collective-defense clause.
The defense pact could also expand beyond its three founding members. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said Egypt is the most likely next member, noting that the four countries already cooperate like alliance partners. Turkey has also said the pact is not directed against any country, including Iran, and does not replace existing alliances.
The Makkah Agreement has inevitably drawn comparisons with the Cold War-era Central Treaty Organization, or CENTO, which included Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, Iraq, and Britain. Although the United States supported CENTO through bilateral defense agreements, it never became a member. The alliance ultimately failed to develop an effective collective defense mechanism and dissolved in 1979 following Iran’s revolution.
That history raises questions about whether the Makkah Agreement could face similar challenges.
For Bangladesh, however, the more immediate question is why it would want to join such a pact.
Dhaka has expressed interest in joining, but it has not received an invitation.
“If they express an intention to include Bangladesh in the pact, we will certainly consider it positively,” Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament on August 27. He also made clear that Bangladesh’s inclusion was not currently under discussion.
That distinction is important. Bangladesh is not joining the Makkah Pact. It is signaling that it would consider joining if invited.
Yet even that signal is politically significant.
The pact brings together three countries with very different strategic interests but substantial military and political weight. For Bangladesh, closer engagement with them could open another channel of diplomacy beyond its traditional relationships with India, China, the United States, and Japan.
But it could also complicate those relationships.
For a developing Asian country like Bangladesh, the central question is simple: What security problem would joining the Makkah Pact actually solve?
Bangladesh does not face the same immediate security environment as Saudi Arabia, Turkey, or Pakistan. It is not in the Middle East and does not face the regional military threats that shaped the pact.
Its security concerns are primarily regional, including its relationship with India, border management, maritime security, and the wider stability of the Bay of Bengal.
Joining a defense pact centered on countries thousands of kilometres away would therefore require a clear strategic justification.
There could be benefits.
Bangladesh is a Muslim-majority country of more than 170 million people and has deep economic and social links with the Gulf.
Millions of Bangladeshis work in the Middle East, making Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states important sources of remittances.
Closer relations could therefore bring economic as well as diplomatic benefits.
The pact could also give Dhaka another platform through which to engage with influential Muslim-majority countries.
But the risks may be greater than the immediate security benefits.
India is likely to watch Bangladesh’s interests in possible participation closely. New Delhi has a longstanding strategic rivalry with Pakistan, while India and Bangladesh share a border of more than 4,000 kilometres.
The growing military ties between Dhaka and Islamabad in the last two years have also raised concerns in New Delhi. India has previously accused Bangladesh of allowing northeastern Indian insurgents to operate from its territory, allegedly with Pakistani support. Bangladesh and Pakistan denied those allegations.
For Dhaka, the challenge is therefore to deepen ties with Pakistan and the wider Muslim world without allowing India to see the move as a strategic alignment against it.
India is Bangladesh’s neighbour and cannot be replaced by a distant strategic partner. Saudi Arabia is an important economic and religious partner, but it cannot offer Bangladesh what India does simply because of geography.
Pakistan, meanwhile, carries its own complicated history with Bangladesh.
The Makkah Pact could nevertheless give Rahman additional diplomatic space if he uses it as part of a broader strategy of diversification. But if it becomes a perceived anti-India or pro-Pakistan alignment, it could create exactly the kind of regional tensions Bangladesh has traditionally sought to avoid.
This is where the political gamble lies.
For Rahman, the Makkah Pact could also prove to be a politically useful card at home, particularly for mobilizing support among anti-India groups and Bangladesh’s Muslim majority ahead of Hasina’s planned return.
And in Bangladesh, this kind of political symbolism is not unusual.
Even former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina was given the title “Qawmi Janani,” or “Mother of Qawmi,” ahead of the 2018 general elections after her government formally recognized Qawmi madrasa degrees.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman also met Hefazat Ameer Shah Muhibullah Babunagari in Chittagong on August 9, asking the religious pressure group to continue its support for the BNP.
With this signal on the Makkah Pact, it would not be surprising if a new slogan emerged on the streets of Dhaka: “Delhi or Makkah? Makkah, Makkah.” Whether such a slogan actually emerges remains to be seen, but the political narrative is already taking shape.
The move could help bring the pro-July forces together to counter the Awami League as Hasina’s expected return in December approaches.
In fact, BNP’s calculated view toward Makkah, and its attempt to connect Bangladesh’s foreign policy with the symbolism of Islam’s holiest city, could do more than solidify the position among Islamist groups, even the parliamentary opposition party Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, which has welcomed the idea of Bangladesh considering participation in the pact.
And that could certainly become a political test of Sheikh Hasina’s determination to return to Dhaka.
In Bangladesh’s complex political landscape, where religion and politics remain deeply intertwined, this diplomatic dance carries consequences far beyond international relations.
For Tarique Rahman, it is a gamble over both foreign policy and domestic political supremacy.
Sardar Ronie is a Bangladesh-based journalist with nearly 16 years of experience covering politics, human rights, and regional issues for international outlets including BBC News, DW Asia, and Al Arabiya English, bringing stories from the ground to global audiences. He can be reached at sardarronie@gmail.com .

Pakistan fined, docked 11 WTC points for slow over-rate in Birmingham Test. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan have been fined 50 per cent of their match fee, and penalised 11 World Test Championship points for maintaining a slow over-rate during the third and final Test against England in Birmingham, the International Cricket Council (ICC) said on Monday.

In a press release, the ICC said Pakistan were ruled to be 11 overs short of the target after time allowances were taken into consideration during the match.

“Ranjan Madugalle of the Emirates ICC Elite Panel of Match Referees imposed the sanction, after on-field umpires Paul Reiffel and Chris Gaffaney, third umpire Allahudien Palekar and fourth umpire Russell Warren levelled the charge,” the cricketing body said.

It said that Pakistan were now sitting at the bottom of the World Test rankings, with 4.63 points percentage. Pakistan were previously at the bottom of the rankings, with 14.81 points percentage.

As per ICC rules, a side is penalised one point for each over short. In addition, players are fined five per cent of their match fee for each over their team fails to bowl within the allotted time, with the maximum penalty capped at 50pc of the match fee.

The Test, which concluded on Saturday, saw England complete a comprehensive 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan, winning the last match by eight wickets.

In May, Pakistan were penalised 40pc of their match-fees as well as eight World Test Championship points for maintaining a slow over-rate during a Test match against Bangladesh.

item.title: What Bangladesh should ask before joining the Makkah Pact. [ dawn ]
item.description:
BANGLADESH is suffering the consequences of a Middle East war that continues to drag on, like many other countries dependent on imported energy. In June, QatarEnergy warned that it might ship only 20 of the 40 cargoes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) expected this year, and officials returned to buying gas through emergency tenders at higher prices. But this is only part of the story.

The war has exposed just how much of the country’s economic wellbeing depends on the Gulf. Three-quarters of the Bangladeshis who went abroad for work between FY2015 and FY2025 went to the Middle East, and close to half of the country’s remittances come from the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states. This is the backdrop against which Dhaka is weighing the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, which Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan signed on August 7. Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman has already told parliament that the government would consider an invitation positively.

Whether Bangladesh should join at all is a separate debate. But if the government decides to align itself with Saudi Arabia, it has an opportunity to negotiate the terms before signing. Nothing should be given away for free: Bangladesh should leverage its alignment to secure commitments on its migrant workers, skills development, energy security and investment.

Of course, the obvious question is: why would Saudi Arabia listen? Because the Kingdom is building a coalition, and there is strength in numbers. The Pact’s signatories have said it is open to other states. Bangladesh has already joined a Saudi-led maritime alliance of 14 countries covering the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, and on September 2, its defence adviser discussed expanded military training exchanges and disaster management cooperation with the Saudi ambassador. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected to travel to Riyadh at the crown prince’s invitation. A country that is being courted has bargaining power, and that power is greatest before it signs. Once the ink is dry, every request becomes a favour.

The very first ask should be to secure the livelihoods of one of Bangladesh’s most valuable economic assets: its migrant workforce. According to BMET, more than 9.69 lakh Bangladeshis left for overseas jobs in FY2025 -26, the lowest figure in five years. Recruiters say Saudi Arabia is now the only market in the Middle East that is still actively hiring, but that landscape is rapidly shifting. The Kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund has dropped large-scale projects from its 2026-30 strategy and cut some project budgets by up to 60 percent, while growth in the number of registered construction workers in the Kingdom slowed from 32 percent in 2025 to 6 percent in the first quarter of 2026.

A World Bank study found that more than 60 percent of Bangladeshi migrants abroad work in construction, putting the country’s workers—and a major source of foreign remittances—at risk. The employment agreement the two countries signed in October 2025, which promised stronger protections, guaranteed wages and better welfare, needs to be backed by firm targets and a clear pathway for skilled workers.

Protecting these jobs, however, requires more than baseline quotas; it demands a joint commitment to upskilling. Saudi Arabia now requires low-skilled foreign workers to pass its Takamul skill verification before they can be hired, and in October 2025, as the requirement took hold, departures from Bangladesh fell by 18.46 percent. Bangladesh now tests roughly 60,000 workers each month across 28 centres. That is progress, but the cost of meeting Riyadh’s standards falls largely on the workers themselves, who pay about $50 for each test, while the state pays for training programmes to prepare them.

If the Kingdom wants skilled labour, it should share that cost. The October 2025 agreement already bars agencies and employers from charging workers unauthorised fees; extending that principle to testing fees, while co-funding training and testing centres in Bangladesh, would be a modest next step. But the real payoff lies beyond construction sites. As the Gulf races to build data centres and cloud infrastructure, it needs network engineers and IT technicians. A joint digital skills initiative could finally help move Bangladeshi workers beyond predominantly manual labour and into higher-skilled, higher-earning occupations.

Beyond labour, Dhaka’s most pressing domestic vulnerability remains its energy sector. This year has shown how little protection Bangladesh’s long-term gas contracts can offer when supplies come under pressure. Dhaka has now secured $3.3 billion in financing from the Jeddah-based International Islamic Trade Finance Corporation to pay for fuel, gas and fertiliser this fiscal year.

Saudi Arabia does not sell gas to Bangladesh, but Saudi Aramco supplies crude oil to the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (BPC), and the Kingdom is the largest shareholder in the Islamic Development Bank Group, of which the trade finance corporation is part. A deferred-payment facility for oil imports and access to cheaper Islamic trade finance could do more to strengthen Bangladesh’s energy security than almost any diplomatic gesture.

Whatever terms it secures in Riyadh, Dhaka must also protect what it already has elsewhere in the Gulf. More than a million Bangladeshis live in the UAE. Visa processing for most categories of Bangladeshi applicants has been effectively frozen since 2024, while remittances from the UAE fell by more than 10 percent in 2025, to $4.16 billion. The Makkah Pact has also drawn criticism from prominent commentators in the UAE, giving Bangladesh another reason to tread carefully.

The government has so far played down concerns about how joining the pact might affect relations with other states. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has described the expanded pact as an internal Muslim matter carrying no foreign policy risk, maintaining that there is no reason for concern. That may be good diplomatic messaging, but it is not a strategy.

Moving closer to Riyadh requires Bangladesh to pursue parallel diplomatic tracks across the Gulf to safeguard its migrant workforce and broader economic interests. Dhaka should consider putting forward similar strategic asks to Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and the UAE, with the normalisation of visa processing in the UAE as an immediate priority. Crucially, these relationships—along with vital gas supplies from Qatar and Oman—must not become collateral damage in any new arrangement with Riyadh.

None of these demands is unreasonable given what Bangladesh has already contributed to the Gulf. For decades, Bangladeshi workers have poured the concrete that built its cities, often in punishing heat and for modest wages, while sending home the remittances that have helped carry their own country through one economic shock after another. If Bangladesh is now prepared to offer Saudi Arabia its political alignment as well, it should make sure that alignment advances its own national interests.

Published in Dawn, September 14th, 2026

item.title: Can the RMG sector maintain its position in the global apparel market?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh’s ready-made garment (RMG) industry stands at a critical juncture. The sector generates over 80% of the country’s export earnings while supporting millions of livelihoods. However, global competitiveness now extends beyond cost, quality, and delivery to include sustainability, transparency, responsible business practices, and credible environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance.
The key question is whether Bangladesh can move beyond a compliance-driven mindset and leverage sustainability practices and reporting as strategic tools to strengthen its position in the global apparel market.
The RMG sector transformed significantly after the 2013 Rana Plaza tragedy, which exposed critical weaknesses in workplace safety, labour compliance, and factory governance. In response, the industry adopted widespread reforms supported by global initiatives, regulatory authorities, and international buyers.
These reforms led to significant improvements in workplace safety, structural integrity, labour standards, and environmental management. Bangladesh now hosts the world’s largest number of LEED-certified green garment factories. Many manufacturers have also adopted energy-efficient technologies, wastewater treatment, water recycling, and renewable energy systems, demonstrating the sector’s growing commitment to sustainable manufacturing.
Despite these achievements, Bangladesh operates in an increasingly competitive global apparel market. Increasing competition from Vietnam, India, and Turkey highlights the need to strengthen competitiveness beyond low-cost production. Future success will depend on sustainability performance, innovation, supply-chain transparency, and resilience rather than price alone.
Global sustainability transformation requires organizations to integrate sustainability practices with credible sustainability reporting through a structured five-step roadmap. The process begins with assessment and governance, where organizations identify material ESG risks using double materiality and align priorities with the UN SDGs.
Photo: Courtesy
Next, sustainability is embedded into operations through carbon measurement, Scope 3 emissions management, renewable energy, circular production, labour rights, and supply chain traceability.
These practices respond to evolving global regulations. The roadmap then focuses on performance monitoring using measurable ESG indicators and science-based climate targets (SBTi). Finally, organizations disclose sustainability performance through frameworks such as GRI and SASB supported by external assurance.
Together, sustainability practices and reporting enhance accountability, market access, investor confidence, and the long-term competitiveness of Bangladesh’s RMG sector.
Over the past two decades, sustainability has become a core requirement in global apparel supply chains. International brands increasingly require compliance with standards on labour rights, occupational safety, environmental management, and responsible sourcing.
Frameworks such as GRI, the Higg Index, and ZDHC have accelerated the adoption of cleaner technologies, wastewater treatment, resource-efficient production, and stronger monitoring systems across factories. Industry leaders increasingly recognize that long-term competitiveness depends not only on compliance but also on embedding sustainability into core business strategy.
A key pillar of this transformation is sustainability reporting. Leading Bangladeshi manufacturers have begun publishing sustainability and ESG reports using internationally recognized frameworks. These early adopters reflect growing alignment with global expectations and increasing institutional maturity across the sector.
Sustainability reporting strengthens buyer confidence, improves operational efficiency, supports access to green finance, and enhances risk management. It also enables manufacturers to benchmark performance and identify opportunities for continuous improvement.
However, progress remains uneven across the industry. While large exporters are increasingly adopting structured reporting, many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) still lack the technical expertise, financial resources, and data management systems needed for comprehensive reporting.
As a result, they continue to rely on fragmented disclosures driven by buyer audits, certifications, and compliance requirements.
This gap reduces transparency, limits comparability, and raises concerns about data reliability across the value chain.
Although sustainability reporting is not yet mandatory for all manufacturers, it is expected to become a formal requirement by 2027 as global regulatory frameworks evolve.
Bridging this gap will require coordinated efforts to strengthen technical capacity, improve digital infrastructure, and expand access to affordable green finance.
Despite significant progress, several structural challenges continue to limit the full sustainability transformation of Bangladesh’s RMG industry.
One major challenge is the sector’s continued reliance on fossil-fuel-based energy systems, which restricts large-scale emissions reduction. Although some factories have adopted renewable energy solutions, the national energy structure remains carbon intensive.
Access to green finance is another key constraint, especially for SMEs investing in cleaner technologies, wastewater treatment, and digital reporting systems. High initial costs often delay sustainability investments despite their long-term benefits.
Environmental management practices also vary across the sector. While leading factories use advanced wastewater treatment and chemical management systems, many production clusters still face challenges in textile waste management and circular economy adoption.
Labour-related challenges also remain, including wages, worker representation, skills development, and human rights due diligence. Manufacturers must also navigate complex buyer requirements, certification schemes, and regulatory frameworks, which can increase audit fatigue and compliance costs.
To remain globally competitive, Bangladesh’s RMG sector must move beyond compliance-driven sustainability and establish sustainability as a core business strategy.
This requires stronger governance, improved reporting systems, and integration of ESG priorities into corporate decision-making, risk management, and investment planning.
Wider adoption of global reporting frameworks, independent assurance mechanisms, and digital traceability solutions will be essential to improve transparency, credibility, and data quality across the value chain.
At the same time, an inclusive sustainability transition will require targeted support for SMEs through technical assistance, capacity building, and access to affordable green finance.
Collaboration among manufacturers, global brands, policy-makers, financial institutions, development partners, and academic institutions will be critical to overcome barriers and accelerate industry-wide transformation.
Bangladesh’s RMG industry has demonstrated its ability to adapt by improving workplace safety, strengthening compliance systems, and advancing sustainable factory practices.
However, the next stage of competitiveness will depend on transforming sustainability from a set of operational initiatives into a measurable and strategic advantage.
As global apparel sourcing increasingly prioritizes carbon performance, resource efficiency, transparency, human rights, and accountability, cost competitiveness alone will no longer be sufficient.
The central challenge now for Bangladesh is to institutionalize credible sustainability reporting and ensure that responsible practices are embedded throughout the industry.
By doing so, Bangladesh can strengthen buyer confidence, secure long-term market access, and maintain its position as a global apparel leader.
Mohammad Rabiul Kabir is an associate professor at Stamford University, Bangladesh, and a sustainability and ESG professional.

item.title: Towards stronger ties with France. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
At a time when the Bangladesh economy is experiencing a particularly challenging period, it is more important than ever to strengthen our diplomatic relations with nations.
To that end, the visit of the French Senate delegation and their expressed interest in deeper political engagement with Bangladesh is an important moment, and one that Dhaka should seize with clarity and ambition.
France, beyond being a major European power, is also a strategic actor in global security, climate diplomacy, and development cooperation. Strengthening ties with Paris serves Bangladesh’s long‑term interests, especially as we navigate our economic and social challenges in a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape.
The senators’ remarks signal that France sees Bangladesh as more than a development partner and views it as a country with growing regional influence and a role to play in Indo‑Pacific dynamics.
This recognition matters and opens the door to more robust cooperation in areas where France has deep expertise: defense modernization, renewable energy, climate expertise, digital governance, and higher education.
Bangladesh, for its part, has every reason to welcome this interest. France has been a consistent supporter of Bangladesh, be it the climate agenda, infrastructure development, or being a growing market for Bangladeshi goods.
With Bangladesh eventually needing to shed its LDC tag, stronger political engagement with France can help diversify partnerships, expand trade opportunities, and strengthen diplomatic leverage in the entirety of Europe.
Bangladesh, for its part, must articulate clear priorities, from technology transfer and green energy investment to cultural exchanges. Engagement must also move beyond courtesy visits and translate into structured dialogue, joint initiatives, and long‑term agreements.
Bangladesh has the opportunity to deepen a relationship built on mutual respect and shared global concerns with a major European nation. We must not squander it. Stronger ties with Paris will not only enhance Bangladesh’s international standing but also support its aspirations for sustainable development, climate resilience, and eventually, a more prosperous future.

item.title: The non-residential Bangladeshi: Reform or ruin?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is an old, unwritten law: You can take a Bangladeshi out of the country, but you can rarely extract the country from the Bangladeshi.
When a person steps off a flight at Heathrow or JFK, a silent internal split occurs.
The passport changes, the currency in the wallet shifts, but the underlying psychological software -- that intricate, centuries-old wiring shaped by deltaic floods, agrarian survivalism, and localized territoriality -- remains intact.
This raises an uncomfortable, introspective question: Does life abroad genuinely elevate the non-resident Bangladeshi (NRB) psyche, or does it merely provide a grander, more lucrative stage for domestic vices?
There is a comforting, widely peddled myth popular in living rooms across Dhaka and Chittagong: That the average Bangladeshi, notoriously prone to skipping queues and bribing their way out of trouble back home, magically transforms into a law-abiding saint the moment they step foot into a Western nation.
The argument usually points to the omnipresent "rule of law" -- the strict speed cameras, the unbribable police, the automated tax audits, and the certainty of punishment.
In Bangladesh, institutional fragility turns law into an optional menu of suggestions; abroad, it is assumed, the sheer weight of enforcement forces instant moral reform.
Yet, public record reveals a far more complicated psychological reality. The rule of law certainly creates external compliance, but it does not automatically erase decades of ingrained survival instincts.
For a significant cohort, the presence of a structured, trusting system does not inspire civic duty -- it merely changes the nature of the game.
Where law back home is evaded through brute influence or financial bribes, abroad it is often tested through administrative loophole-hunting, calculated anonymity, and systemic arbitrage.
To trace the psychological shifts of the diaspora, one must look at the historical trail left in the press and legal archives.
The migration waves of the 1980s and 1990s -- particularly to the United Kingdom and Southern Europe -- brought not just workforce muscle, but also the instinctual survival mechanisms of the homeland.
In the late 1980s and through the 1990s, British media periodically highlighted complex welfare and housing benefit scams originating out of East London’s Tower Hamlets -- a hub heavily settled by Sylheti families.
What local authorities framed as sophisticated "social security fraud" was often, at its core, the psychological extension of shonchoy (survival hoarding) and system-gaming honed in a home country where state institutions were meant to be bypassed, not trusted.
By the mid-2010s, investigative operations in Europe laid bare even stranger phenomena: Operations where Bangladeshi migrants holding Italian passports were flying into London on day trips to lodge fraudulent welfare claims before flying back out.
In Australia, immigration reports over the decades have quietly documented cash-in-hand wage undercutting, pseudo-marriages for permanent residency, and localized rental "hot-bedding" schemes run by established diaspora landlords exploiting newly arrived countrymen.
To the foreign observer, these act as felonies or administrative crimes.
But to an introspective Bangladeshi, they are recognizable reflexes.
The rule of law deters blatant chaos, but it cannot prevent the scarcity-driven impulse to extract maximum resources with minimal exposure.
When we look into the mirror, we see ancestral traits that refused to dissolve in foreign waters.
Take the stereotypical Noakhali ethos: Fiercely hardworking, notoriously tight-knit, possessing an innate commercial shrewdness, and an uncompromising loyalty to the clan.
When transported to London’s Brick Lane, New York’s Jackson Heights, or Sydney’s Lakemba, this trait morphs into an enclave mentality.
It creates vibrant business ecosystems, but it can also create isolated echo chambers where Western civil code is treated as an external inconvenience, and the primary moral obligation remains owed strictly to one's immediate lineage back home.
Conversely, consider the Barisal archetype: Deeply opinionated, intellectually pugnacious, and harbouring an ingrained skepticism toward formal authority -- a product of living in a riverine landscape where land itself shifts overnight.
Overseas, this manifests as a refusal to quietly assimilate.
It can express itself as political factionalism -- where Bangladeshi political rivalries are absurdly re-enacted in municipal hall meetings -- or as an instinctive urge to find the hidden loophole in any structured bureaucracy.
Yet, to characterize the NRB experience solely through its missteps is to miss a profound psychological evolution.
Migration is a pressure cooker. While the weak points of the psyche can rupture into criminality under stress, its strengths -- when paired with actual rule of law -- can crystallize into extraordinary global achievement.
For those who genuinely allow the structural stability of foreign nations to alter their internal compass, the transformation is real:
For these individuals, living abroad broke the chain of scarcity mindsets.
It replaced the anxiety of bluffing through life with genuine mastery, allowing the inherent warmth, hospitality, and intelligence of the Bangladeshi character to shine through without the corrupting friction of institutional decay.
Does the non-resident Bangladeshi change for the better or the worse? The truth is that migration acts as a magnifier, not an automatic moral cleanser.
The presence of the rule of law creates a fork in the road rather than a guaranteed transformation.
If a person departs Bangladesh viewing rules merely as obstacles to dodge, foreign soil simply provides a more stable, lucrative infrastructure to game.
The bad gets worse because the safety nets of wealthy nations offer higher stakes to exploit.
However, if a person uses the predictability of foreign law to shed the hyper-vigilance required to survive back home, the Bangladeshi psyche undergoes a remarkable transformation.
The raw energy used for survival converts into an unmatched work ethic. The clannish loyalty expands into genuine civic responsibility.
The NRB remains forever caught between two worlds: Carrying the river's chaos in their blood, while deciding whether to respect or exploit the paved, orderly streets of the world.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Getting serious about dengue prevention. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s inauguration of the three‑month nationwide dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign is a reminder once again that Bangladesh cannot afford complacency when it comes to the disease.
Dengue continues to claim lives while hospitals remain strained, and the next three months are considered the highest‑risk period. The PM’s message is clear and one that ought to have been heeded years ago: Dengue cannot be controlled by mosquito‑killing drives alone; it requires public awareness, daily vigilance, and collective responsibility.
The campaign’s emphasis on keeping surroundings clean and removing stagnant water every day reflects the core truth of dengue prevention. Aedes mosquitoes breed in small, overlooked pockets of water -- flowerpots, rooftop corners, discarded containers, construction sites, and household drains.
No city corporation, no ministry, and no volunteer force can eliminate these breeding grounds without active participation from residents.
The PM’s call for coordinated field‑level activities involving local administrations, volunteers, students, and community groups recognizes that dengue prevention must be woven into everyday life.
Around 25,000 volunteers have reportedly already joined the campaign, and this sort of intent shown is the kind of energy we need to turn this campaign into a success.
Yet, while weekly visits to homes and establishments will help identify breeding sites and raise awareness, their efforts will only succeed if households respond -- by cleaning regularly, checking rooftops and balconies, clearing drains, and refusing to let water accumulate.
The PM’s directive to intensify awareness campaigns across television, mass media, and social media underscores the urgency of changing public behaviour, not just public policy.
We have continued to struggle with dengue because prevention has often been reactive, triggered only after outbreaks worsen. This campaign must mark a shift toward proactive, sustained action.
Dengue is preventable. Bangladesh must prove that it can prevent it.

item.title: Pakistan to open FIFA ASEAN Cup campaign against Thailand. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan start their FIFA ASEAN Cup campaign against Thailand on Sept 26 after being drawn in Group ‘B’ of Division One for the inaugural tournament, which will take place later this month with matches played in Indonesia and Hong Kong, organisers said on Thursday.

The 11 members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and three guest sides — Hong Kong, Pakistan and Bangladesh — will play in two divisions from Sept 24 .

Eight teams will contest the top-tier Division 1 — hosts Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Vietnam, Bangladesh and Pakistan .

They will be split into two sections of four with the winners contesting the first FIFA ASEAN Cup final on Oct 5 .

Pakistan have been placed in Group ‘B’ alongside Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam .

The Green Shirts face the Philippines on Sept 29 before their final group-stage fixture against Vietnam on Oct 2.

Pakistan entered the tournament after China withdrew from the inaugural edition to focus on preparations for the 2027 Asian Cup and 2030 World Cup qualifiers.

Pakistan will enter the competition on a high after winning the Diamond Jubilee Intern­ational Football Tournament in the Maldives earlier this year, their first standalone international title since 1952.

The second-tier Division 2 will be hosted by Hong Kong and also involve Brunei, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Timor-Leste, split into two three-team sections with the winners advancing to a final on Oct 3 .

“The FIFA ASEAN Cup was launched to provide national teams with meaningful competitive opportunities,” said FIFA president Gianni Infantino. “The tournament will strengthen football ties across Southeast Asia.”
